DOCUMENT:
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432." -- Maintenance and licensing (£67,200) has been added to gross labour savings (£1,051,232) instead of subtracted. Correct net savings are £1,051,232 - £67,200 = £984,032, so payback on £1,344,000 is about 16.4 months, not 'about 14 months'.
2. [inconsistency] at: "Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:" -- The document elsewhere says the pilot ran in four stores and names them (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley); here the results are attributed to three pilot stores. The pilot store count contradicts itself.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit." -- Pilot stores were not randomly chosen: the document says they were selected because they had just been fully refurbished in early 2025 (and were larger). Refurbishment and store selection are obvious confounders for basket growth, so the comparison cannot show that self-checkout caused larger baskets.

REVIEW:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion Business Case

The case is clearly structured and the pilot data is useful. However, there is an arithmetic error in the core financials, and a confound in the pilot design weakens several of the headline claims. Both should be fixed before this goes to the Committee, especially since the paper says Finance has reviewed the model.

## 1. Net savings are overstated: maintenance was added, not subtracted

Section 5 says "after maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432." But:

- Gross labour savings: £1,051,232
- Plus maintenance: £67,200 = **£1,118,432** (the figure in the paper)
- Minus maintenance: £67,200 = **£984,032** (the correct figure)

Payback is therefore £1,344,000 ÷ £984,032 ≈ **16.4 months**, not 14. The case still clears the 24-month hurdle, so the conclusion survives. But an error in the central number will damage credibility once someone spots it. It also needs correcting in the recommendation ("little over a year") and in your summary.

The gross calculation itself checks out: 95 × £15.20 × 52 × 14 = £1,051,232.

## 2. "Three pilot stores" vs four

Section 2 names four pilot stores, but Section 3 says "Across the **three** pilot stores." Either this is a typo, or one store was dropped from the results. If a store was excluded, the Committee will want to know which one and why, because excluding an underperformer would bias every figure in the table. Please resolve this explicitly.

## 3. The pilot stores were freshly refurbished, which confounds the results

The pilot stores were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025. That means they differ from the comparison stores in two ways at once: new kiosks and a newly refurbished store. This matters most for:

- **Basket value (+6% vs +2%).** New layouts, ranging and fixtures commonly lift basket size. The paper says the pilot "shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit." The data cannot support that causal claim. I'd recommend:
  - removing the word "shows" and the "three times as fast" framing;
  - dropping basket value from the recommendation's list of benefits, or at most calling it "an encouraging but unproven signal";
  - comparing against other refurbished stores without kiosks, if any exist.
- **Satisfaction (+7 points).** The same refurbishment confound applies.
- **Queue times** are more plausibly driven by the kiosks, but refurbishment may still contribute.

Leaving basket value out of the numbers was the right call. But the narrative still leans on it, and a sceptical Committee member will raise the refurbishment point straight away.

## 4. The pilot results may not transfer to the 14 remaining stores

- **Floor space.** Pilot stores were picked partly because they could fit six kiosks *without removing shelving*. The remaining 14 may not have that space. If they don't, there are fit-out costs and lost selling space that the £9,000-per-store installation quote may not cover. Please confirm the quote is based on site surveys of these 14 stores.
- **Store size.** The rollout is "sequenced by store size," which suggests the stores vary a lot. Applying a flat 95 hours per week to every store assumes each one has about 790 front-end hours a week. Smaller stores will likely save less, and some may not justify six kiosks. A store-by-store savings estimate, or at least a sensitivity line, would make the case much more robust.

## 5. Labour savings vs redeployment

The paper says the pilot reductions came partly through "redeployment of colleagues into online order picking." Redeployed hours are only a saving if those picking hours would otherwise have been filled by new hires. If not, the cost has just moved to another budget line. Please state how much of the 95 hours was turnover and how much was redeployment, and confirm that the £15.20 saving is a real reduction in total payroll.

On the redundancy point, 38% turnover against a 12% hours reduction looks comfortable on average. However, turnover is uneven across stores and through the year, and the rollout completes within about six months. "We do not expect to need a consultation process" is reasonable. "No redundancy risk," as your summary puts it, is stronger than the evidence supports.

## 6. Gaps in costs and risks

- **No contingency** on capital. Typical practice is 5–10%.
- **Asset life.** What is the expected kiosk life? Payback means little without knowing whether the kiosks last 5 years or 10.
- **One-off costs** are missing: staff training, trading disruption during installation, and signage.
- **Shrink sensitivity.** Shrink is reported to 0.1 percentage point. On a typical store's annual sales, a 0.1pp rise could offset a large share of that store's £75k saving. Industry experience is that self-checkout shrink often rises after the first year. A sentence quantifying this, plus a commitment to keep monitoring, would strengthen the risk section.

## 7. Suggested sensitivity table

A small table showing payback under different savings assumptions would help the Committee judge the risk. Based on the corrected figures:

| Hours saved per store per week | Net annual saving | Payback |
|---|---|---|
| 95 (pilot) | £984k | 16.4 months |
| 75 | £762k | 21.2 months |
| 65 | £651k | 24.8 months (misses hurdle) |

This shows the case holds up to roughly a 30% shortfall in hours saved. That is a useful and honest message, and more persuasive than "low-risk."

## Summary of required changes

1. Correct net savings to £984,032 and payback to about 16 months throughout.
2. Resolve the three vs four pilot stores discrepancy.
3. Acknowledge the refurbishment confound, and soften or remove the basket-value causal claim.
4. Confirm the installation quotes reflect floor space in the 14 remaining stores, and consider store-level savings estimates.
5. Clarify how much of the saving is redeployment versus real payroll reduction.
6. Add contingency, asset life, one-off costs, a shrink sensitivity and a payback sensitivity table.

With these fixes, the case is still a sound one to approve. It will just rest on numbers that will hold up under scrutiny.
